units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Let's start with a puzzle, Ben.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: When was Luxembourg born?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Depends who you ask. Some people say 1815, when the Grand Duchy was created at the Congress of Vienna.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Others say 1839, when its modern borders were drawn in London.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Others point to 1867, when the great powers guaranteed its independence.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But you have a different answer.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The story we're telling really starts in the year nine sixty-three, with an exchange of land beside a river.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And before that exchange, there are thousands of years we shouldn't skip.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who's our first character?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He has no name. Archaeologists call him Loschbour man, after the rock shelter near the village of Heffingen where his skeleton was found in 1935.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He lived about eight thousand years ago, when this land was covered in dense forest and people survived by hunting, fishing, and gathering.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And his DNA made headlines.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Decades after his discovery, when scientists sequenced it, the result suggested that this early European had dark skin and blue eyes, a combination that overturned a lot of assumptions about what the first Europeans looked like.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who came after him?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Farmers, who arrived from the southeast and cleared fields along the river valleys.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then the age of metal, first bronze and later iron.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By the last centuries before Christ, the land of Luxembourg belonged to a Celtic people called the Treveri.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And they left a monument.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A fortified hilltop town called the Titelberg, in the far southwest of today's country, close to the French border.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It sat on a high plateau, with ramparts around it, and it was a center for metalworking and trade.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Imagine a town of craftsmen and warriors, with a view across the countryside, and one of the richest cavalry traditions in Gaul.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then Rome arrives.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The first written reference to this territory comes from Julius Caesar himself, in his account of the Gallic Wars.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Around the middle of the first century before Christ, Caesar fought the Treveri, and after years of rebellion and repression, the region was swallowed into the Roman Empire.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the Romans built a city nearby.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the Moselle river, just across what's now the German border: Augusta Treverorum, today's Trier.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Within a few generations it became one of the great cities of the western empire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At one point it was the home of emperors, and its Roman gates and baths still stand.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So what was Luxembourg's role?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Trier's backyard. Farmland and forest, crossed by Roman roads and dotted with country estates.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of those roads ran from the city of Reims, in what's now France, to Trier.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Along it, near today's village of Dalheim, grew a small Roman town with a theater.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And villas.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At Echternach and at Diekirch, wealthy landowners built grand villas.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At Diekirch, a Roman mosaic from one of those houses survives, laid out in colored stone.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Life was settled, Latin-speaking, and for a few centuries, secure.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the empire cracked.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the third and fourth centuries, raiders pushed across the Rhine, and Roman power along the frontier began to wear away.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By the end of the fifth century, the region had passed to the Franks, a Germanic people whose king, Clovis, was building a new kingdom out of the ruins of Roman Gaul.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Luxembourg's land became part of the Frankish heartland, in the eastern half that was later called Austrasia.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Christianity came with them.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: With a handful of remarkable missionaries.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The most important for our story is a monk named Willibrord, born in Northumbria, in England, and trained in Ireland.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He crossed the sea to preach to the pagan Frisians, and in the year six ninety-eight he founded a monastery at Echternach, on land given to him by a noblewoman from the Trier area.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Willibrord died in the year seven thirty-nine and was buried there.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Echternach became famous, didn't it?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of the great intellectual centers of medieval Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its monks copied and illuminated manuscripts so beautiful that they're treasured today in museums in Germany.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there's the dancing procession.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Every year, on the Tuesday after Pentecost, thousands of people dance through the streets of Echternach, hopping in time to a simple polka-like tune, in honor of Saint Willibrord.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: UNESCO now recognizes it as part of humanity's living cultural heritage.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then we reach Charlemagne.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the late eighth and early ninth centuries, the Frankish kings became emperors, and the Echternach region sat comfortably inside their realm.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But when Charlemagne's empire was split among his grandsons by the Treaty of Verdun in eight forty-three, the land that would become Luxembourg fell into the middle kingdom, named after the grandson Lothar.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that didn't last.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Over the following decades it broke up, and the region we're talking about became a borderland, a long-contested strip between the western Frankish kingdom, which would become France, and the eastern Frankish kingdom, which would become Germany.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then a new emperor.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the year nine sixty-two, in Rome, a German king named Otto was crowned emperor.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His realm would later be known as the Holy Roman Empire, a loose, shifting collection of kingdoms, duchies, counties, and church lands that would last for more than eight hundred years.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And just one year later, a count named Siegfried made a small land deal that no one at the time could have thought important.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who was Siegfried?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He belonged to a noble family from the Moselle and Ardennes region, and according to tradition he had Carolingian blood.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: What he wanted was a stronghold.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the edge of lands he controlled, there was a rocky promontory rising above the river Alzette, with the ruins of an old fortification.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which belonged to someone else.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: To the abbey of Saint Maximin in Trier.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Siegfried offered other lands in exchange, and the monks agreed.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the charter survives.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Dated nine sixty-three. It gives the name of the place: Lucilinburhuc, which means roughly little castle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In time, the name would shorten and soften into Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the rock itself?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It would later be known as the Bock.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Siegfried built a real fortress on it, and from there his family would spread out across the surrounding land.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The place was so well chosen that armies would fight over it for the next nine hundred years.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there's a legend, of course.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Of course. It says that Siegfried married a mermaid named Melusina, who agreed to live with him on the condition that he never look at her on a certain day.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He broke the promise, and she vanished beneath the waters of the Alzette, leaving him alone.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And locals say she can still be seen.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Once every seven years, spinning at the bottom of the river.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the real story is better than the legend.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I think so. Because from this small rocky outcrop, Siegfried's descendants would rise to the heights of European power.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They would sit on the throne of Bohemia and wear the imperial crown.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In the next chapter, we meet the House of Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And it's quite a family.
